blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Load Balancing. **Goal:** know every way to add capacity, and the failure modes of each.

rows: Bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disk

blocks.text: **Vertical first, then horizontal.** Most systems never need to be distributed: a single Postgres handles 10–50k writes/sec with proper indexing. Scale up until that's not enough, then shard.
The failure mode is the opposite: teams shard at 100 RPS because microservices "sound senior", then spend a year debugging distributed bugs and running 30 services for 5 users.
**The single most important scaling decision: make your application servers stateless.**
State on a server instance means:

items.text: The instance is not interchangeable → load balancer must do **sticky sessions** (affinity).
You can't scale down or restart without losing state.
Deploys require draining.
Autoscaling can't evict safely.

blocks.text: Move state to a shared store (Redis, Postgres, S3) or to the client (tokens, JWTs). Then:

items.text: Any instance can serve any request.
Rolling deploys are trivial.
Autoscaling is safe.
Horizontal scaling is just "add N".

blocks.text: What "state" really means
A common senior-level nuance: "stateless" doesn't mean "no state anywhere." It means *no instance-local authoritative state*. Local caches and read-only config are fine.
Where state *should* live sometimes: sticky sessions
Sticky sessions are legitimate when:

items.text: The session payload is large and moving it is expensive.
Connection affinity to a specific backend is required (WebSocket, DB connection).

blocks.text: If you need affinity, prefer a **consistent-hash affinity** layer (Envoy/Kong/HAProxy) over "round-robin + cookie" — it spreads load by request hash rather than by session creation order.

sections.title: 3. What a load balancer actually does

blocks.text: L4 vs L7 load balancing

rows: Pooled: N client conns → M backend conns

blocks.text: **Rule of thumb:** L4 for internal traffic and raw TCP/UDP (databases, gRPC with HTTP/2 multiplexing still usually L7-aware); L7 for public HTTP APIs, where you want routing, TLS, and maybe caching.
Routing algorithms

rows: Route to least busy work queue

blocks.text: Health checks and failure detection

items.text: **Liveness**: "is the process alive?" → restart if it fails. Must **not** check dependencies, or a

blocks.text: database blip restarts every instance simultaneously and makes the outage worse.

items.text: **Readiness**: "can this instance serve traffic *right now*?" → remove from rotation if it fails.

blocks.text: This *should* check dependencies (or at least, a critical subset).

items.text: **Startup probe**: "has it finished booting?" → prevents slow starts from being killed.

blocks.text: **The thundering-herd restart** is a classic: liveness probe = `GET /health` which checks the DB. DB has a 30-second blip → every instance fails liveness → all restart at once → all try to connect to a cold DB → overload → longer outage. Never put a shared dependency in a liveness check.
Active/passive vs active/active

rows: Split brain if promotion is racy

blocks.text: **Active/passive is for stateful components** (a Postgres primary, a Kafka leader). **Active/active is for stateless app tiers.** You can also do active/active with Postgres using multi-primary with conflict resolution, but that brings a large complexity bill — see [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md).
**Scaling on a schedule** is predictable; **scaling on a metric** reacts. Good systems use both.
The signals

rows: Memory/IO-bound services look idle; slow to react
Doesn't account for cost per request
Best as a *secondary* signal (autoscaling on latency alone oscillates)

blocks.text: **Prefer concurrency over CPU.** A service doing 2-second IO-bound calls can be at 100% CPU util... no wait, at 10% CPU while being completely saturated. Scale on in-flight requests, not CPU. This is one of the most common real-world scaling mistakes.
The three things that break autoscaling

items.text: **Slow scale-out**: the metric spikes, but new instances take 60s to boot. Fix: reduce startup time (pre-baked images, lazy init) and scale on leading indicators (queue depth, scheduled events).
**Oscillation** (scale out → load drops → scale in → load returns → repeat). Fix: longer scale-in stabilization windows, coarser metrics, and asymmetric scale policies.

**Nothing to scale** — the bottleneck is the DB, not the app tier. Autoscaling 100 app servers against 1 saturated Postgres makes the DB worse, not better. **Always ask: what is the actual bottleneck?**

blocks.text: Scale-down safety
Before killing an instance, a good platform:

items.text: Stops sending new requests (readiness → false).
Waits for in-flight requests to drain (grace period).
Allows the process to checkpoint/flush local state.

sections.title: 5. DNS, Anycast, and global load balancing

blocks.text: DNS-based

items.text: Cheap, universal, but **TTL-cached** → changes take minutes to propagate, and clients ignore

blocks.text: TTLs. Clients and intermediate resolvers cache aggressively.

items.text: Use for: pointing at a stable LB VIP, not for fine-grained traffic engineering.

blocks.text: Anycast

items.text: The same IP announced from many locations; the network routes you to the nearest (BGP).
Used by: Cloudflare, AWS Global Accelerator, Google.
Amazing for: static/CDN-ish content and UDP services (DNS, QUIC, game servers).
Caveat: it's *network-level* — you can't do L7 routing, and flow state can be asymmetric.

blocks.text: L7 global load balancer / geo-routing

items.text: Path-based: `/us/...` → US backend, `/eu/...` → EU backend.
Latency-based: send to the region with the lowest latency *for this client*.
Data residency: send EU users to EU storage — **a legal requirement, not an optimization**.
Weighted: 95% stable, 5% canary. This is how you do a safer production deploy.

blocks.text: Connection draining on deploys

blocks.code:
1. LB marks instance "draining" (no new requests)
2. Wait for in-flight to complete (or force-close after grace period)
3. Graceful SIGTERM → app stops accepting, finishes work
4. SIGKILL after timeout (last resort)

blocks.text: Rolling deploy with N instances: replace ~10% at a time, wait for health, continue. Never replace all at once — you'd drop all capacity.

sections.title: 6. Connection pools and the thundering herd

blocks.text: A classic failure: **DB connection exhaustion**.

blocks.code:
Scenario: 50 app instances × 100 DB connections each = 5,000 connections.
Postgres max_connections = 3,000.
→ 2,000 requests fail immediately. Traffic is fine; the DB is the wall.

blocks.text: Rules:

items.text: **Every** DB client pools. Set `max_connections` per instance so that `instances × pool ≤ DB limit`,

blocks.text: with headroom for migrations and admin tools.

items.text: **Set a connect timeout.** A request that can't get a connection in 50ms should fail fast, not

blocks.text: hang for 30s. Hanging requests consume the caller too, and the failure spreads.

items.text: **Bound total concurrency at every hop.** Thread pools, connection pools, semaphore limits.
**Prefer a queue with a limit over an unbounded queue.** 10,000 queued requests each holding a

blocks.text: connection will collapse the system; a 100-deep queue with 503 responses degrades gracefully.
**Backpressure** is the practice of pushing back on callers when you're saturated. Every hop must implement it, or overload propagates and collapses the whole system instead of one component.
When you're overloaded, you must decide who to serve. Options:

rows: Fails some requests, protects the rest
Disable recommendations, serve stale cache, drop logging
Serve 1 in 10 requests, cache the rest (protects DB, hurts correctness)

blocks.text: **Timeouts must be hierarchical.** If the API times out at 3s, it must pass a smaller timeout (e.g. 1s) to the DB. Otherwise when the DB slows down, requests pile up in the app tier waiting and every layer fails at once.

**Retry storms**: when a dependency recovers, all clients that timed out retry simultaneously. Mitigations: **exponential backoff with jitter**, **retry budgets**, and **circuit breakers** that stay open for a while after a failure rather than flapping.

sections.title: 8. Stateless + Cache + Autoscale + LB — the standard shape

blocks.text: Note the properties this buys you: any instance can serve any request; deploys are rolling; a crashed instance is replaced in seconds; traffic spikes are absorbed by the autoscale group; the DB is protected by the cache.

items.text: **LB simulator.** Write a small program that distributes 1,000,000 requests with variable durations (1ms–2s) across N nodes using: round-robin, least-connections, and power-of-two-choices. Report the p99 of the *response time* for each. Watch round-robin suffer.
**Detect the thundering herd.** Write two instances that both poll a shared counter with a 1s interval, and add a "leader election" (a lock). Show the difference in DB load before/after.

**Boot a stateless service.** Deploy something trivial (a 3-line HTTP server) behind a local LB with 3 instances, hit it 1000 times, and prove the responses come from different instances (return the instance ID). Then add a sticky-session cookie and observe the difference.

**Autoscale math.** A service processes requests with 50ms latency. Target: keep p99 < 200ms with 1000 RPS. Each instance handles 200 RPS. How many instances at steady state? How many at 3x spike? What's the minimum to survive one instance dying?

blocks.text: Strong answers include:

items.text: "I'll start with a stateless service tier behind an L7 load balancer; state goes to Redis/Postgres."
"I'll scale on in-flight requests rather than CPU, because the workload is IO-bound."
"Readiness checks dependencies; liveness checks only the process, so a DB blip doesn't restart

blocks.text: everything at once."

items.text: "I'll use a connection pool sized so instances × pool < DB max connections, with a connect timeout."
"At 10x I'd add cache and read replicas; the write path becomes the bottleneck, so I'd shard by user ID."

blocks.text: Red flags:

items.text: Sticky sessions as the default answer.
"Autoscaling solves scale" without identifying the real bottleneck.
Liveness checks that hit the database.
Unbounded queues.

selfCheck.q: **Why must liveness probes not check shared dependencies?**
selfCheck.a: If the DB blips and liveness depends on it, every instance fails liveness at once and restarts simultaneously — turning a dependency blip into a full outage, plus a cold-cache thundering herd on recovery. Liveness should only test the process itself.

selfCheck.q: **What breaks if 50 instances each open 100 DB connections and the DB allows 3,000?**
selfCheck.a: 5,000 connections attempted against a 3,000 limit → ~2,000 requests fail to connect; the app tier's concurrency collapses. Fix: pool per instance, size `instances × pool ≤ limit` with headroom, and set a short connect timeout so failures are fast.

selfCheck.q: **A service is IO-bound, CPU sits at 10%, and p99 is climbing. Which autoscaling signal is best?**
selfCheck.a: **In-flight request concurrency** (or request rate). CPU is a poor signal for IO-bound work: the instance is saturated while looking idle. Scaling on CPU would under-provision; scaling on latency alone oscillates, so pair it with concurrency.

selfCheck.q: **Vertical vs horizontal scaling — give one case where vertical is strictly better.**
selfCheck.a: When the whole workload fits on one machine and the problem is a single hot spot (a large in-memory dataset, a big join) — vertical scaling has no coordination overhead and no distributed-systems bugs. Also when the team can't operate distributed infrastructure yet.

selfCheck.q: **What is the difference between readiness and liveness, and what happens if you swap them?**
selfCheck.a: Readiness = "can serve traffic now" → LB removes the instance from rotation. Liveness = "is the process wedged" → the platform kills and restarts it. Swapping them means a temporarily overloaded instance gets restarted (losing in-flight work) while a dead-but-liveness-passing instance stays in rotation.

selfCheck.q: **Why can DNS be a poor load-balancing mechanism?**
selfCheck.a: DNS responses are cached by clients, browsers, and resolvers for the TTL, and many clients ignore TTLs entirely. So changes propagate in minutes, not seconds; you lose fine-grained routing; and DNS-based failover can leave a large fraction of clients pointing at a dead IP. Use DNS for coarse steering (region), L4/L7 LB for actual request routing.

selfCheck.q: **Your service calls a dependency that takes 30s. Your API timeout is 3s. What goes wrong?**
selfCheck.a: Requests pile up in the app tier for up to 30s while the app's own 3s timeout should have fired. You get connection-pool exhaustion, unbounded memory growth, and a fail-slow collapse. Fix: **hierarchical timeouts** (app→dependency timeout < app's own deadline), bounded pools, and circuit breakers.

selfCheck.q: **What is "fail-slow" and why is it worse than "fail-fast"?**
selfCheck.a: Fail-slow means requests queue instead of failing, so latency and memory explode and the whole service goes down — the failure spreads to callers. Fail-fast rejects immediately, preserving capacity for the requests that can succeed. Fix with bounded queues, timeouts, and backpressure.

selfCheck.q: **How do you deploy a new version with zero downtime on an N-instance fleet?**
selfCheck.a: Rolling deploy: replace instances in batches (~10% of the fleet), marking each drained instance not-ready, waiting for in-flight requests to complete, sending SIGTERM, waiting for graceful shutdown, and verifying health before continuing to the next batch. Keep at least one full batch of capacity serving throughout.

selfCheck.q: **The DB is at 100% CPU. The app tier is at 20%. You add 50 app instances. What happens?**
selfCheck.a: **Nothing improves; it gets worse.** The bottleneck is the DB, so 50 more app instances send 50x more concurrent queries at an already-saturated DB, exhausting connections and pushing latency up. The correct move is to reduce DB load (cache, read replicas, denormalization, async writes) or scale the DB — not the app tier.
